questions.question: What best describes cloud computing?

choices.text: Delivering computing services such as servers, storage and databases over the internet
Storing every file only on one personal laptop
Building a physical data centre inside your own home
Using a computer that is never connected to a network

questions.explanation: Cloud computing provides on-demand access to computing resources over a network, usually the internet, so you do not need to own and run all the hardware yourself.

b.why: Keeping files on one laptop is local storage. Cloud computing delivers services over a network, usually the internet.

c.why: Building your own data centre means owning the hardware, which is the opposite of renting computing services from a provider.

d.why: Cloud services are reached over a network, so a computer that is never connected cannot use them.

questions.question: When a company moves from buying its own servers to using cloud services, which spending model does it mainly shift toward?
questions.explanation: Cloud services are typically paid for as ongoing usage costs (OpEx) instead of large upfront hardware purchases (CapEx).

a.why: CapEx is the large upfront purchase of hardware, which is exactly what moving to the cloud moves away from.

c.why: Cloud services are billed on an ongoing basis according to use, not as a single purchase.

d.why: The cloud still costs money. You pay for what you use instead of buying hardware upfront.

questions.question: Which term describes a service remaining accessible and running with minimal downtime?
questions.explanation: High availability means designing a service so it stays up and reachable as much of the time as possible.

a.why: Portability is about moving workloads or data between environments, not about staying online.

b.why: Archiving stores old data cheaply for the long term. It does not keep a service running.

d.why: Encryption protects data from being read by others. It does not keep a service available.

questions.question: What does scalability mean in the cloud?

choices.text: Making applications look bigger on screen
Copying data to a USB drive
The ability to increase or decrease resources to meet demand

questions.explanation: Scalability lets you add or remove resources such as compute power or storage as workload needs change.

a.why: Scalability is about computing capacity, not how an application looks on screen.

b.why: Copying data to a USB drive is a manual backup, not adjusting resources to demand.

c.why: Turning services off can save money, but scalability means adjusting resources up or down to match demand.

questions.question: Which feature best describes elasticity?

choices.text: Permanently reserving a fixed number of servers
Automatically adding and removing resources as demand rises and falls

questions.explanation: Elasticity is automatic scaling out and in with demand, so you only run what you need at a given time.

a.why: A fixed number of reserved servers cannot grow or shrink with demand, which is the opposite of elasticity.

c.why: Backups protect data. Elasticity is about automatically matching resources to demand.

d.why: Encryption protects data. It has nothing to do with adjusting resources to demand.

questions.question: Which cloud benefit refers to a system's ability to recover from failures and keep working?
questions.explanation: Reliability is the ability of a system to recover from failures and continue to function.

b.why: Predictability is about forecasting performance and costs, not recovering from failures.

c.why: Agility is about how quickly you can deploy and change resources.

d.why: Portability is about moving workloads between environments.

questions.question: A finance team wants to forecast cloud costs and performance accurately in advance. Which cloud benefit supports this?
questions.explanation: Predictability covers both performance and cost, helping organizations plan and forecast what they will need and spend.

a.why: Elasticity automatically adjusts resources to demand. It helps control costs but is not about forecasting them.

b.why: Disaster recovery is about restoring services after an outage, not forecasting costs.

d.why: Fault tolerance keeps a system running when parts fail. It does not help forecast costs.

questions.question: In an Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) deployment, who is responsible for patching the guest operating system?
questions.explanation: In IaaS the provider manages the physical infrastructure, while the customer manages the operating system, applications and data.

a.why: In IaaS, Microsoft manages the physical hosts, network and datacenter, but not the operating system inside your VM.

b.why: Your internet provider only supplies your connection. It has no access to your Azure VMs.

c.why: Update tools exist, but someone has to set them up and manage them. In IaaS that is the customer.

questions.question: Which description fits a public cloud?

choices.text: Services owned and operated by a cloud provider and shared across multiple customers
Servers used by only one company inside its own building
A cloud that is accessible to nobody
A cloud that works only without internet

questions.explanation: A public cloud is owned and operated by a provider, with resources shared among many customers on isolated tenants.

b.why: Servers used only by one company in its own building describe a private cloud or on-premises datacenter.

c.why: A cloud nobody can access would be useless. Public clouds are available to anyone who signs up.

d.why: Public cloud services are reached over the internet, not without it.

questions.question: Which description fits a private cloud?

choices.text: Hardware rented by the hour from a provider by anyone
A free service for the general public
Cloud resources used exclusively by a single organization
A cloud that cannot store data

questions.explanation: A private cloud is dedicated to one organization and can be hosted in its own datacenter or by a third party.

a.why: Hardware rented by the hour to anyone describes the public cloud.

b.why: A private cloud serves one organization, not the general public, and it is not free.

d.why: A private cloud stores data like any other cloud. What makes it private is that only one organization uses it.

questions.question: What is a hybrid cloud?

choices.text: A cloud with only one server
A combination of public and private cloud or on-premises environments working together
A cloud that works only on mobile phones
A cloud that is turned off at night

questions.explanation: Hybrid cloud connects public cloud with private or on-premises resources so they can work together.

a.why: The number of servers does not define hybrid cloud. Hybrid means combining public cloud with private or on-premises resources.

c.why: Hybrid cloud has nothing to do with the type of device people use.

d.why: Hybrid cloud is about combining environments, not about operating hours.

questions.question: Which is an example of Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)?

choices.text: A word processor delivered in a browser

questions.explanation: Virtual machines give you raw compute infrastructure that you configure and manage, which is the IaaS model.

b.why: Ready-to-use software in a browser is SaaS, not IaaS.

c.why: An email service you subscribe to is SaaS: finished software, not infrastructure.

d.why: A printed manual is not a cloud service at all.

questions.question: Which is an example of Platform as a Service (PaaS)?

choices.text: A physical server in your office
A subscription to a hosted email product
A virtual machine you manage fully
Azure App Service hosting a web app

questions.explanation: PaaS lets you deploy applications while the provider manages the underlying servers, operating system and runtime.

a.why: A physical server in your own office is on-premises, not a cloud service.

b.why: A hosted email product is SaaS: finished software you use, not a platform you deploy your own apps to.

c.why: A virtual machine you manage fully is IaaS, because you look after its operating system.

questions.question: Which is an example of Software as a Service (SaaS)?

choices.text: Microsoft 365 email and office apps used through a subscription

questions.explanation: SaaS delivers complete, ready-to-use software; the provider manages almost everything.

a.why: A virtual network is infrastructure you configure yourself, which is IaaS.

c.why: A bare-metal server is raw infrastructure, not finished software.

d.why: A cable is physical hardware, not a cloud service.

questions.question: What best describes serverless computing?

choices.text: Computing with no servers existing anywhere
Running code without managing the servers, with the provider handling infrastructure and scaling

questions.explanation: Serverless still uses servers, but the provider manages them so developers focus on code. Azure Functions is an example.

a.why: Serverless still runs on servers. You just do not manage them; the provider does.

b.why: Serverless code runs in the cloud and is usually triggered over the network, so it is not offline.

d.why: With serverless, the provider owns and manages the hardware, not you.

questions.question: What does the consumption-based pricing model mean?

choices.text: You pay for the resources you actually use
You pay a fixed fee regardless of use

questions.explanation: Consumption-based pricing means you pay for what you use, with no large upfront cost.

b.why: A fixed fee regardless of usage is the opposite of consumption-based pricing.

c.why: With consumption-based pricing you pay for the services you use, not for buying hardware.

d.why: Cloud services are not free. You pay for what you use.

questions.question: Why can large cloud providers often offer lower prices per unit than a small company running its own datacenter?

choices.text: Economies of scale from buying and operating resources in very large quantities

questions.explanation: Providers purchase and operate at massive scale, which lowers cost per unit and can be passed on to customers.

a.why: Datacenters use huge amounts of electricity. Providers save through scale, not by avoiding it.

b.why: Providers run modern hardware. Lower prices come from buying and operating at very large scale.

c.why: Lower prices come from economies of scale, not from avoiding taxes.

questions.question: A startup needs to launch a test environment in minutes instead of weeks. Which cloud benefit does this show?
questions.explanation: Cloud resources can be provisioned quickly on demand, helping teams move faster.

a.why: Owning hardware is what slows teams down. The cloud lets you use resources without buying them.

c.why: Manual installation takes time. The benefit here is fast, on-demand provisioning.

d.why: Long procurement cycles are the problem the cloud solves, not the benefit.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of disaster recovery in the cloud?

choices.text: To reduce the number of users
To restore services and data after an outage or disaster
To remove the need for backups

questions.explanation: Disaster recovery plans and tools help an organization restore operations and data after a serious disruption.

a.why: Performance is a separate concern. Disaster recovery is about restoring services after a serious disruption.

b.why: Disaster recovery aims to keep serving users, not to reduce them.

d.why: Disaster recovery depends on backups and replicas. It does not replace them.

questions.question: Under the shared responsibility model, which responsibility always stays with the customer regardless of service type?

choices.text: Their data and who has access to it
The power supply of the datacenter

questions.explanation: Customers are always responsible for their data, identities and access, even when using SaaS.

b.why: The physical datacenter building is always the cloud provider's responsibility.

c.why: Physical network cables are always managed by the cloud provider.

d.why: Datacenter power is always the cloud provider's job.

questions.question: What does fault tolerance mean?

choices.text: A system continuing to operate even when some of its components fail

questions.explanation: A fault-tolerant system keeps running when a component fails, usually through redundancy.

a.why: Ignoring errors does not keep a system running. Fault tolerance relies on redundant components.

b.why: Fault tolerance is about the system tolerating failures, not users tolerating poor service.

c.why: Removing a failed server is not enough on its own. Fault tolerance means other components take over so the system keeps working.

questions.question: A business in Kenya wants customers in Europe to get fast access to its application. Which cloud benefit helps most?

choices.text: Global reach through datacenters in many regions

questions.explanation: Cloud providers operate datacenters worldwide, letting you deploy close to your users.

a.why: One server in Kenya would be far from users in Europe, which makes access slower.

c.why: Brochures do not affect how fast an application responds.

d.why: Screen size has nothing to do with application speed.

questions.question: Which is a security benefit of using a major cloud provider?

choices.text: The provider invests heavily in physical datacenter security and security tooling

questions.explanation: Providers protect datacenters physically and offer security tools, but customers still share responsibility for secure configuration.

a.why: Passwords and identity protection are still needed. Security in the cloud is shared.

b.why: Cloud data is private by default unless you choose to share it.

d.why: No system is immune to attack. Customers still need to configure their resources securely.

questions.question: Which scenario is a good reason to choose a hybrid cloud?

choices.text: Keeping sensitive data on-premises while using the public cloud for extra capacity
Wanting to stop using all networks

questions.explanation: Hybrid cloud lets organizations keep regulated or sensitive workloads local while still using cloud scale for other needs.

b.why: Hybrid cloud depends on networks to connect on-premises and cloud resources.

c.why: Hybrid cloud has nothing to do with avoiding backups, which every organization needs.

d.why: Printed records are not a cloud model at all.

questions.question: An online shop expects a huge traffic spike during a holiday sale and a quiet period afterwards. Which cloud capability fits best?

choices.text: Buying servers sized for the peak permanently
Closing the shop in the busy season
Scaling resources out for the spike and back in afterwards

questions.explanation: Elastic scaling lets you add resources for peak demand and release them later, reducing wasted cost.

a.why: Servers sized for the peak sit idle the rest of the year, wasting money. The cloud lets you scale only when needed.

b.why: Closing during the busiest period would lose sales. Scaling handles the extra demand instead.

c.why: The goal is to serve every customer by adding resources when demand rises.

questions.question: Compared with IaaS, what does the provider additionally manage in PaaS?

choices.text: The operating system and runtime environment

questions.explanation: In PaaS the provider also manages the operating system and runtime so you focus on applications and data.

a.why: Your data is always your responsibility, in every service type.

c.why: Managing your users' credentials and access stays with you.

d.why: Business decisions are never the cloud provider's responsibility.

questions.question: What is vertical scaling?

choices.text: Adding more machines to share the load
Moving servers to a taller building
Adding more CPU or memory to an existing resource

questions.explanation: Vertical scaling (scaling up) increases the power of an existing resource, such as a larger VM size.

a.why: Adding more machines is horizontal scaling (scaling out).

b.why: Vertical scaling is about the size of a resource, not the height of a building.

d.why: Deleting servers removes resources, but vertical scaling changes the size of an existing resource.

questions.question: What is horizontal scaling?

choices.text: Adding more instances of a resource to share the workload
Rewriting an application in a new language

questions.explanation: Horizontal scaling (scaling out) adds more instances, such as additional VMs, to handle more load.

b.why: Horizontal scaling adds more instances. It does not change a server's physical size.

c.why: Reducing network speed makes things slower and is not scaling.

d.why: Rewriting code is not scaling. Scaling changes the resources that run the application.

questions.question: What is an Azure region?

choices.text: A set of datacenters deployed within a latency-defined area and connected by a low-latency network

questions.explanation: A region is a geographic area containing one or more datacenters where you can deploy resources.

a.why: A rack is a tiny part of one datacenter. A region contains one or more whole datacenters.

c.why: Regions are physical locations, not account types.

d.why: A region is a geographic area where resources run, not a report.

questions.question: What are Azure availability zones?

choices.text: Physically separate locations within a region, each with independent power, cooling and networking

questions.explanation: Availability zones protect applications from datacenter-level failures by spreading resources across separate locations in a region.

a.why: Availability zones are physical locations, not time zones.

b.why: Availability zones are datacenter locations, not email groups.

c.why: Pricing tiers set cost and features. Availability zones are separate physical locations in a region.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of Azure region pairs?

choices.text: Supporting disaster recovery by pairing regions in the same geography
Offering two prices for one service
Pairing two users to one account

questions.explanation: Each region is paired with another in the same geography so some services can replicate data and recover from large-scale disasters.

b.why: Region pairs are about disaster recovery, not pricing.

c.why: Region pairs link two regions, not two users.

d.why: Subscriptions are billing and access boundaries. Region pairs link two regions for recovery.

questions.question: What is an Azure resource group?

choices.text: A logical container that holds related Azure resources

questions.explanation: Resource groups organize related resources so they can be managed, deployed and deleted together.

a.why: A virtual machine is a resource that lives inside a resource group.

b.why: Invoices come from your billing account. A resource group organizes resources.

d.why: A resource group is a container for resources, not a credential.

questions.question: What is an Azure subscription?

choices.text: A unit that provides a boundary for billing and access to Azure resources

questions.explanation: A subscription links to an account and provides authenticated access to resources, along with billing boundaries.

a.why: A subscription is an Azure billing and access boundary, not a publication.

c.why: A disk is a resource. A subscription is the boundary that contains resources.

d.why: A virtual network is a resource that lives inside a subscription.

questions.question: What is the purpose of Azure management groups?

choices.text: To organize and apply governance across multiple subscriptions

questions.explanation: Management groups sit above subscriptions, letting you apply policies and access controls to many subscriptions at once.

b.why: Management groups organize Azure subscriptions, not staff.

c.why: Management groups have nothing to do with keyboards.

d.why: Files are stored in storage accounts. Management groups organize subscriptions for governance.

questions.question: What is Azure Resource Manager (ARM)?

choices.text: The deployment and management service for Azure resources

questions.explanation: ARM is the management layer that lets you create, update and delete resources through the portal, CLI, PowerShell, SDKs and templates.

a.why: ARM manages Azure resources, not printers.

b.why: ARM is a cloud management layer, not a device monitor.

c.why: Cost estimates come from the pricing calculator. ARM deploys and manages resources.

questions.question: Which Azure service lets you run a full operating system in the cloud that you manage yourself?
questions.explanation: Azure Virtual Machines are IaaS compute resources where you control the operating system and software.

a.why: Azure DNS hosts domain name records. It does not run an operating system.

b.why: Key Vault stores secrets and keys. It does not run an operating system.

d.why: Advisor gives recommendations. It does not run virtual machines.

questions.question: Which Azure feature automatically creates and manages a group of identical, load-balanced virtual machines?
questions.explanation: Scale sets let you deploy identical VMs that can automatically increase or decrease in number with demand.

b.why: Resource locks protect resources from deletion or changes. They do not create VMs.

c.why: Azure Policy enforces rules on resources. It does not create or scale VMs.

d.why: Advisor makes recommendations. It does not manage groups of VMs.

questions.question: What do availability sets help protect against?

choices.text: Hardware failures and planned maintenance within a datacenter

questions.explanation: Availability sets spread VMs across fault domains and update domains to reduce the impact of hardware faults and maintenance.

a.why: Availability sets are about keeping VMs running, not about billing.

c.why: Password strength is handled by identity features, not availability sets.

d.why: Licensing has nothing to do with availability sets.

questions.question: A developer wants to host a web application without managing the underlying servers. Which service fits best?
questions.explanation: Azure App Service is a PaaS offering for hosting web apps, APIs and mobile backends.

a.why: Data Box is a physical device for moving large amounts of data to Azure.

b.why: Azure Migrate assesses and moves existing workloads to Azure. It does not host web apps.

c.why: Azure DNS resolves domain names. It does not host the application itself.

questions.question: Which Azure service runs small pieces of code in response to events, such as a file upload, without managing servers?
questions.explanation: Azure Functions is an event-driven serverless compute service.

a.why: A virtual network connects resources. It does not run code.

b.why: Azure Files provides file shares. It does not run code.

d.why: ExpressRoute is a private network connection. It does not run code.

questions.question: Which service lets you run a container quickly without managing virtual machines or an orchestrator?
questions.explanation: Azure Container Instances runs containers on demand with no VM management.

a.why: Table storage holds structured NoSQL data. It does not run containers.

c.why: Azure Monitor collects metrics and logs. It does not run containers.

d.why: Azure Policy enforces rules. It does not run containers.

questions.question: Which Azure service is used to deploy and manage containerized applications with Kubernetes orchestration?
questions.explanation: AKS is a managed Kubernetes service that simplifies deploying and operating containerized applications.

b.why: Azure DNS resolves domain names. It does not orchestrate containers.

c.why: Azure Backup protects data. It does not run containerized applications.

d.why: Blob Storage stores unstructured data. It does not orchestrate containers.

questions.question: Which service delivers cloud-hosted Windows desktops and apps to users remotely?
questions.explanation: Azure Virtual Desktop is a desktop and app virtualization service running in the cloud.

a.why: Cost Management tracks spending. It does not deliver desktops.

b.why: Blueprints package governance settings for repeatable environments. They do not deliver desktops.

c.why: Service Health reports Azure outages and maintenance. It does not deliver desktops.

questions.question: What is an Azure Virtual Network (VNet) used for?

choices.text: Creating a private, isolated network in Azure where resources can communicate

questions.explanation: VNets let Azure resources communicate securely with each other, the internet and on-premises networks.

a.why: Billing data is handled by Cost Management, not virtual networks.

b.why: Files are stored in storage accounts. A virtual network is for communication between resources.

d.why: Virtual networks do not send email. They connect resources privately.

questions.question: Which service creates an encrypted connection over the public internet between an on-premises network and Azure?
questions.explanation: VPN Gateway sends encrypted traffic across the public internet between networks.

b.why: Azure Files provides file shares, not network connections.

c.why: Advisor gives recommendations, not network connections.

d.why: Data Box moves data by shipping a physical device, not through an encrypted network connection.

questions.question: How does Azure ExpressRoute differ from a VPN connection?

choices.text: It is a free service for everyone
It uses a private connection that does not travel over the public internet
It only works with mobile phones

questions.explanation: ExpressRoute provides a dedicated private connection through a connectivity provider, often with more reliability and predictable performance.

a.why: ExpressRoute is a paid service, usually arranged through a connectivity provider.

c.why: ExpressRoute connects networks, such as an office or datacenter, to Azure. It is not for phones.

d.why: ExpressRoute is a network connection. It does not store data.

questions.question: Which feature filters inbound and outbound network traffic to Azure resources using rules?
questions.explanation: NSGs contain security rules that allow or deny network traffic based on source, destination, port and protocol.

a.why: Blob storage stores data. It does not filter network traffic.

b.why: Advisor recommends improvements but does not filter network traffic.

c.why: Cosmos DB is a database. It does not filter network traffic.

questions.question: Which service hosts your domain name records and resolves names using Azure infrastructure?
questions.explanation: Azure DNS hosts DNS domains and provides name resolution.

a.why: Azure Backup protects data. It does not host domain records.

b.why: Azure Monitor collects telemetry. It does not resolve domain names.

d.why: Azure Migrate helps move workloads to Azure. It does not host DNS records.

questions.question: Which service distributes incoming network traffic across multiple virtual machines to improve availability?
questions.explanation: A load balancer spreads traffic across healthy instances so no single VM is overwhelmed.

b.why: Key Vault stores secrets. It does not distribute traffic.

c.why: Azure Policy enforces rules. It does not distribute traffic.

d.why: Azure Files provides file shares. It does not distribute traffic.

questions.question: Which Azure Storage service is designed for large amounts of unstructured data such as images and videos?
questions.explanation: Blob storage stores massive amounts of unstructured data like documents, media and backups.

a.why: Queue storage holds messages between application components, not large media files.

c.why: Azure DNS resolves domain names. It does not store files.

d.why: Azure Virtual Desktop delivers desktops. It is not a storage service.

questions.question: Which service provides fully managed file shares accessible using the SMB protocol?
questions.explanation: Azure Files offers managed cloud file shares that can be mounted like traditional network shares.

a.why: Cosmos DB is a NoSQL database, not a file share service.

b.why: Azure Monitor collects telemetry. It does not provide file shares.

d.why: Advisor gives recommendations. It does not provide file shares.

questions.question: Which Azure Storage service is used to store large numbers of messages for asynchronous processing between application components?
questions.explanation: Queue storage lets application components communicate by passing messages through a queue.

a.why: Blob storage holds unstructured data such as images, not messages between components.

b.why: Azure Files provides file shares, not message queues.

c.why: Azure DNS resolves domain names. It does not store messages.

questions.question: What does locally redundant storage (LRS) do?

choices.text: Keeps three copies of your data within a single datacenter
Copies data to a different continent

questions.explanation: LRS replicates data three times within one datacenter. It is the lowest-cost option but does not protect against a datacenter-wide failure.

b.why: LRS keeps all copies in one datacenter. Copying data to another region is geo-redundant storage (GRS).

c.why: LRS stays within a single datacenter, not across regions.

d.why: Redundancy options keep extra copies of your data. They do not delete it.

questions.question: What does geo-redundant storage (GRS) provide?

choices.text: Replication of data to a secondary region far from the primary

questions.explanation: GRS copies data to a secondary region, protecting against a regional outage.

a.why: Every redundancy option keeps multiple copies. GRS keeps copies in two regions.

c.why: GRS goes much further than one rack: it copies data to a secondary region.

d.why: GRS is not free. It costs more than LRS because it stores more copies.

questions.question: What does zone-redundant storage (ZRS) do?

choices.text: Stores data on a single disk
Replicates data synchronously across availability zones in one region

questions.explanation: ZRS protects data against datacenter-level failure by copying it across availability zones in the same region.

a.why: ZRS keeps copies across several availability zones, not on one disk.

b.why: Archiving is an access tier for rarely used data, not a redundancy option.

d.why: Redundancy options copy data for protection. They do not move it between subscriptions.

questions.question: Which blob access tier is intended for data that is rarely accessed and can tolerate hours of retrieval delay?
questions.explanation: The Archive tier has the lowest storage cost but requires rehydration, which can take hours, before data can be read.

a.why: Hot is for frequently accessed data and has the highest storage cost.

b.why: Premium is a performance tier for fast, low-latency storage, not a tier for rarely accessed data.

c.why: Standard is a performance tier, not an access tier for rarely used data.

questions.question: Which service is a managed relational database offered as PaaS?
questions.explanation: Azure SQL Database is a managed relational database where Microsoft handles patching, backups and high availability.

b.why: Queue storage holds messages, not relational data.

c.why: Advisor gives recommendations. It is not a database.

d.why: Blueprints package governance settings. They are not a database.

questions.question: Which service is a globally distributed, multi-model NoSQL database?
questions.explanation: Azure Cosmos DB provides low-latency, globally distributed NoSQL data storage with multiple APIs.

a.why: Azure Files provides file shares, not a NoSQL database.

b.why: Azure DNS resolves domain names. It is not a database.

d.why: Azure Backup protects data. It is not a database.

questions.question: Which service helps you assess and migrate on-premises servers, databases and applications to Azure?
questions.explanation: Azure Migrate is a central hub for discovering, assessing and migrating workloads to Azure.

a.why: Azure Monitor tracks performance. It does not migrate workloads.

c.why: Azure Policy enforces rules. It does not migrate workloads.

d.why: Key Vault stores secrets. It does not migrate workloads.

questions.question: A company has hundreds of terabytes to move and a slow internet connection. Which option suits this offline transfer?
questions.explanation: Azure Data Box is a physical device shipped to you to transfer large volumes of data to Azure offline.

a.why: Azure DNS resolves domain names. It cannot move large amounts of data.

b.why: Advisor gives recommendations. It cannot move data.

c.why: Azure Monitor tracks performance. It cannot move data.

questions.question: Which tool is a command-line utility for copying data to and from Azure Storage?
questions.explanation: AzCopy copies blobs and files to or from storage accounts using command-line commands.

b.why: Advisor gives recommendations. It is not a command-line copy tool.

c.why: Azure Policy enforces rules. It does not copy data.

d.why: Blueprints package governance settings. They do not copy data.

questions.question: Which Azure service provides cloud-based identity and access management?
questions.explanation: Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure Active Directory) manages user identities and controls access to resources and applications.

a.why: Blob Storage stores data. It does not manage identities.

b.why: A load balancer distributes traffic. It does not manage identities.

d.why: Azure Files provides file shares. It does not manage identities.

questions.question: What does multifactor authentication (MFA) require?

choices.text: Two or more verification methods, such as a password plus a phone prompt
A shared account for the whole team

questions.explanation: MFA combines something you know, something you have, or something you are, making stolen passwords much less useful on their own.

a.why: A longer password is still only one factor. MFA adds a second, different type of proof.

c.why: Typing the same password twice is still just one factor.

d.why: Shared accounts weaken security. MFA is about verifying each individual user.

questions.question: Which feature grants or blocks access based on signals such as user location, device and risk level?
questions.explanation: Conditional Access evaluates signals and applies policies, for example requiring MFA when signing in from an unusual location.

a.why: Data Box is a device for moving data. It does not control sign-ins.

b.why: Advisor gives recommendations. It does not control sign-ins.

c.why: Resource locks protect resources from deletion or changes. They do not evaluate sign-in signals.

questions.question: What is the benefit of single sign-on (SSO)?

choices.text: Users can sign in once and access multiple applications without repeated logins

questions.explanation: SSO improves convenience and can improve security by reducing the number of passwords users must manage.

b.why: Sharing passwords is a security risk. SSO means one sign-in per person, not shared credentials.

c.why: SSO still relies on user identities. It just lets one sign-in cover many applications.

d.why: SSO is about signing in, not about making applications work offline.

questions.question: Which service helps connect, monitor and manage large numbers of Internet of Things (IoT) devices?
questions.explanation: Azure IoT Hub is a managed service for secure, two-way communication between IoT devices and the cloud.

a.why: Azure Files provides file shares. It does not manage IoT devices.

c.why: Azure DNS resolves domain names. It does not manage IoT devices.

d.why: Azure Backup protects data. It does not manage IoT devices.

questions.question: Which tool lets you estimate the cost of Azure services before deploying them?
questions.explanation: The Azure pricing calculator estimates the monthly cost of the services and configuration you select.

a.why: Advisor makes recommendations for resources you already run. It does not estimate costs before you deploy.

c.why: Azure Monitor tracks how running resources perform, not what they will cost.

d.why: Key Vault stores secrets. It does not estimate costs.

questions.question: A company wants to compare the cost of running workloads on-premises with the cost of running them in Azure. Which tool helps?
questions.explanation: The TCO calculator compares estimated on-premises costs with Azure costs over time.

a.why: Azure DNS resolves domain names. It does not compare costs.

b.why: Azure Files provides file shares. It does not compare costs.

c.why: Azure Policy enforces rules. It does not compare costs.

questions.question: Which service helps you monitor, analyze and control Azure spending?
questions.explanation: Microsoft Cost Management helps you track usage and costs, create budgets and find opportunities to save.

b.why: A load balancer distributes traffic. It does not track spending.

c.why: Azure DNS resolves domain names. It does not track spending.

d.why: Data Box is a device for moving data. It does not track spending.

questions.question: What are tags in Azure used for?

choices.text: Adding name-value metadata to resources to organize them and track costs

questions.explanation: Tags are key-value pairs, such as Department=Finance, that help organize resources and group costs in reports.

a.why: Tags are labels. Encryption is handled by other features.

b.why: Tags do not affect performance. They are just metadata.

d.why: Tags do not delete anything, although they can help you find resources you no longer need.

questions.question: Which of these can affect the price of an Azure resource?

choices.text: The colour of the Azure portal
The region where the resource is deployed
The time of day the portal is opened

questions.explanation: Pricing varies by region, resource type, size, usage and other factors, so the same service can cost different amounts in different regions.

a.why: The portal's colours have no effect on what resources cost.

c.why: Your keyboard layout has no effect on Azure prices.

d.why: When you open the portal does not change prices. Prices depend on things like region, size and usage.

questions.question: How can a company reduce cost for steady, predictable VM workloads?

choices.text: Using reservations by committing to one or three years of usage

questions.explanation: Azure Reservations offer significant discounts compared with pay-as-you-go when you commit to a term.

a.why: Buying monitors adds cost and has nothing to do with Azure VM pricing.

b.why: Deleting backups saves little and risks losing data. Reservations are the right tool for steady workloads.

c.why: Disabling the subscription would stop the workloads entirely.

questions.question: What does Azure Hybrid Benefit allow you to do?

choices.text: Use eligible on-premises Windows Server or SQL Server licenses with Software Assurance to reduce Azure costs

questions.explanation: Hybrid Benefit lets organizations apply existing licenses to Azure workloads and save on licensing costs.

b.why: Hybrid Benefit lowers licensing costs. Azure is not free.

c.why: Hybrid Benefit is about licenses, not about skipping updates.

d.why: You still need a subscription. Hybrid Benefit only reduces licensing costs.

questions.question: Which VM option offers deep discounts by using unused Azure capacity but can be interrupted when Azure needs the capacity back?
questions.explanation: Spot VMs suit interruptible workloads such as batch jobs, since they can be evicted when capacity is needed.

a.why: Reservations give discounts for committing to steady use, and reserved VMs are not interrupted.

b.why: A dedicated host is a physical server reserved just for you. It costs more, not less.

d.why: Premium disks are faster storage at a higher price, not discounted spare compute.

questions.question: A company wants to ensure resources can only be created in approved regions. Which service enforces this?
questions.explanation: Azure Policy creates, assigns and manages rules that enforce standards and assess compliance across resources.

a.why: Azure DNS resolves domain names. It cannot restrict where resources are created.

c.why: Data Box is a device for moving data. It cannot enforce rules.

d.why: Azure Files provides file shares. It cannot enforce rules.

questions.question: Which feature prevents users from accidentally deleting or modifying a critical resource?
questions.explanation: Resource locks (CanNotDelete or ReadOnly) override user permissions to protect important resources.

a.why: Advisor recommends improvements. It cannot block deletion.

b.why: Tags are labels. They do not protect resources.

c.why: Azure Migrate moves workloads to Azure. It does not protect resources.

questions.question: Which service helps an organization discover, classify and govern its data across on-premises, multi-cloud and SaaS sources?
questions.explanation: Microsoft Purview provides data governance, risk and compliance tools to understand and protect data.

b.why: A load balancer distributes traffic. It does not govern data.

c.why: Azure Virtual Desktop delivers desktops. It does not govern data.

d.why: Azure DNS resolves domain names. It does not govern data.

questions.question: What does Azure role-based access control (RBAC) do?

choices.text: Controls what actions users, groups and apps can perform on Azure resources by assigning roles

questions.explanation: RBAC assigns roles at a chosen scope so people only have the permissions they need.

a.why: RBAC controls permissions, not performance.

b.why: RBAC manages who can do what in Azure, not physical hardware.

d.why: Cost estimates come from the pricing calculator, not RBAC.

questions.question: What does the principle of least privilege mean?

choices.text: Giving users only the minimum permissions needed to do their job

questions.explanation: Least privilege limits damage from mistakes or compromised accounts by restricting access to what is necessary.

a.why: Giving everyone administrator access is the opposite of least privilege.

c.why: Least privilege limits permissions. It does not remove sign-in.

d.why: Shared accounts make it impossible to limit and track each person's access.

questions.question: What does the defense in depth approach use?

choices.text: Multiple layers of protection so that if one fails, others still protect resources

questions.explanation: Layers such as physical security, identity, perimeter, network, compute, application and data work together.

a.why: Relying on one layer is what defense in depth avoids. If that layer fails, nothing else protects you.

b.why: Passwords are only one layer. Defense in depth combines many.

c.why: Physical security is one layer of many, not the whole approach.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the Zero Trust model?

choices.text: Never trust by default; always verify explicitly and assume a breach is possible
Trust everything inside the corporate network
Trust all users who know the Wi-Fi password

questions.explanation: Zero Trust requires verification for every access request instead of assuming anything is safe because of where it comes from.

b.why: Trusting everything inside the network is the old perimeter model that Zero Trust replaces.

c.why: Knowing a Wi-Fi password proves nothing about who someone is. Zero Trust verifies every request.

d.why: Zero Trust depends heavily on verifying identities.

questions.question: Which service provides security posture management and threat protection across Azure and hybrid workloads?
questions.explanation: Microsoft Defender for Cloud assesses your security posture, gives recommendations and helps detect threats.

a.why: Azure DNS resolves domain names. It does not detect threats.

b.why: Azure Files provides file shares. It does not detect threats.

d.why: Data Box is a device for moving data. It does not detect threats.

questions.question: Which service securely stores secrets, encryption keys and certificates?
questions.explanation: Key Vault keeps sensitive values out of application code and controls who can access them.

a.why: A load balancer distributes traffic. It does not store secrets.

c.why: Azure Migrate moves workloads to Azure. It does not store secrets.

d.why: A virtual network connects resources. It does not store secrets.

questions.question: What is the Azure portal?

choices.text: A physical door to a datacenter
A web-based interface for creating and managing Azure resources

questions.explanation: The Azure portal is a graphical web interface for managing resources without writing commands.

a.why: The portal is a website, not a physical entrance.

b.why: You can create and manage VMs in the portal, but the portal itself is not a VM.

c.why: You can view invoices in the portal, but the portal itself is a management interface.

questions.question: What is the Azure CLI?

choices.text: A cross-platform command-line tool for managing Azure resources

questions.explanation: The Azure CLI runs on Windows, macOS and Linux and lets you manage resources using commands and scripts.

b.why: The CLI is software you run in a terminal, not a hardware device.

c.why: Pricing tiers set service levels. The CLI is a management tool.

d.why: You can manage databases with the CLI, but it is not a database itself.

questions.question: Which tool provides cmdlets for managing Azure resources and is popular with administrators who use PowerShell?
questions.explanation: Azure PowerShell offers cmdlets for automating and managing Azure resources.

a.why: Azure Files provides file shares. It is not a scripting tool.

b.why: Azure DNS resolves domain names. It is not a scripting tool.

d.why: Data Box is a device for moving data. It is not a scripting tool.

questions.question: What is Azure Cloud Shell?

choices.text: A browser-accessible shell for managing Azure with Bash or PowerShell

questions.explanation: Cloud Shell gives you an authenticated command-line environment in your browser with common tools preinstalled.

a.why: Cloud Shell is a browser-based command line, not hardware.

c.why: Cloud Shell runs commands. It is not a report.

d.why: Cloud Shell uses a small file share to keep your files, but it is a command-line environment, not a storage tier.

questions.question: Which service lets you manage servers and resources running on-premises, at the edge or in other clouds from Azure?
questions.explanation: Azure Arc extends Azure management and governance to resources outside Azure.

a.why: Azure DNS resolves domain names. It does not manage servers outside Azure.

b.why: Azure Files provides file shares. It does not manage servers outside Azure.

c.why: Advisor gives recommendations for Azure resources. It does not extend management to resources outside Azure.

questions.question: What is infrastructure as code (IaC), such as ARM templates or Bicep, used for?

choices.text: Defining and deploying Azure resources consistently from declarative files

questions.explanation: IaC lets you describe infrastructure in files so deployments are repeatable, version-controlled and consistent.

b.why: Infrastructure as code describes cloud resources in files. It has nothing to do with buildings.

c.why: Infrastructure as code defines resources, not marketing content.

d.why: Infrastructure as code has nothing to do with monitor size.

questions.question: Which service collects and analyzes telemetry such as metrics and logs from Azure resources and applications?
questions.explanation: Azure Monitor helps you understand how applications and resources are performing and respond to issues.

a.why: Azure DNS resolves domain names. It does not analyse telemetry.

b.why: Blob storage can hold logs, but it does not collect or analyse them.

d.why: Azure Migrate moves workloads to Azure. It does not analyse telemetry.

questions.question: Which service tells you about Azure service issues, planned maintenance and health advisories that affect your own resources?
questions.explanation: Azure Service Health gives personalized alerts and guidance when Azure events may affect your resources.

a.why: The pricing calculator estimates costs. It does not report service issues.

c.why: Key Vault stores secrets. It does not report service issues.

d.why: Azure DNS resolves domain names. It does not report service issues.

questions.question: Which service analyzes your Azure resources and gives personalized recommendations on reliability, security, performance, cost and operational excellence?
questions.explanation: Azure Advisor reviews your deployed resources and suggests best-practice improvements.

a.why: Data Box is a device for moving data. It does not give recommendations.

b.why: Azure Files provides file shares. It does not give recommendations.

c.why: Azure DNS resolves domain names. It does not give recommendations.

questions.question: What do Azure Monitor alerts do?

choices.text: Notify you or trigger actions when a defined condition is met, such as high CPU use

questions.explanation: Alerts proactively notify administrators of issues so they can respond quickly.

b.why: Alerts can trigger actions, but their job is to notify you, not to delete resources.

c.why: Alerts do not change prices.

d.why: Alerts do not change anything about regions.

questions.question: What does a service level agreement (SLA) describe?

choices.text: The colour theme of a service
Microsoft's commitments for uptime and connectivity of a service

questions.explanation: An SLA states the expected availability, usually as a percentage, and what remedies may apply if it is not met.

a.why: An SLA is about availability commitments, not appearance.

b.why: An SLA describes how available a service will be, not the size of a datacenter.

d.why: Prices are published separately. An SLA describes uptime and connectivity commitments.

questions.question: If an application depends on two services that each have a 99.9% SLA, what is true of the composite SLA?
questions.explanation: Multiplying the availabilities of dependent services produces a lower combined figure, so adding dependencies reduces the composite SLA unless redundancy is designed in.

a.why: Each dependency adds another chance of failure, so the combined figure goes down, not up.

c.why: No SLA promises 100%, and combining services lowers availability.

d.why: SLAs can be combined by multiplying the availability percentages.

questions.question: What is generally true of services in public preview?

choices.text: They always include a full production SLA
They are not available to anyone
They may lack an SLA and are not generally recommended for production workloads

questions.explanation: Preview features are released for evaluation and feedback and often have limited or no SLA and support.

a.why: Preview services usually do not have a full SLA. That comes with general availability.

b.why: Public preview is open to anyone who wants to try it.

c.why: Some previews are discounted, but services are not permanently free.

questions.question: Where can organizations find compliance and security documentation about Microsoft cloud services?
questions.explanation: The Service Trust Portal provides audit reports, compliance guides and other trust resources.

b.why: DNS settings manage domain names, not compliance documents.

c.why: A virtual machine's desktop holds your own files, not Microsoft's compliance reports.

d.why: A storage account key is a credential for your data, not a source of compliance documents.

questions.question: Which option is a separate Azure cloud built to meet the compliance and sovereignty needs of government customers?
questions.explanation: Azure Government is a physically and logically separate cloud for government agencies and their partners with specific compliance requirements.

a.why: Azure Files provides file shares. It is not a separate cloud.

b.why: Advisor gives recommendations. It is not a separate cloud.

d.why: Key Vault stores secrets. It is not a separate cloud.

questions.question: Which Azure Monitor capability helps developers monitor the performance and availability of live web applications?
questions.explanation: Application Insights collects telemetry such as response times, failures and usage from running applications.

a.why: Azure DNS resolves domain names. It does not monitor applications.

c.why: Data Box is a device for moving data. It does not monitor applications.

d.why: Blueprints package governance settings. They do not monitor applications.

questions.question: A team wants an email warning when monthly Azure spending reaches 80% of its planned amount. What should it configure?

choices.text: A budget with alert thresholds in Cost Management

questions.explanation: Budgets in Microsoft Cost Management can send notifications when actual or forecast spending crosses thresholds you set.

a.why: Virtual network peering connects networks. It does not track spending.

b.why: A resource lock prevents deletion or changes. It cannot warn you about spending.

c.why: Changing a storage tier can lower costs, but it does not send spending warnings.
